tweets.text:
Global smartphone purchases have collapsed.

Worldwide smartphone shipments dropped -22.0% YoY in Q3 2026, to 255.3 million units, their largest quarterly decline on record.

Samsung's shipments fell -5.8% YoY, to 57.8 million units, while Apple's declined -4.0% to 57.3 million units.

At the same time, Xiaomi shipments fell -29.2% YoY to 30.7 million units, Oppo dropped -34.5%, to 25.6 million units, while Vivo fell -31.5%, to 19.1 million units.

This comes as memory costs have surged +350% since last year, driven by AI-related demand, putting further pressure on smartphone manufacturers.

As a result, soaring component costs are forcing vendors to raise prices and reduce budget-focused offerings, with consumers increasingly keeping their existing devices for longer.

Global smartphone sales are contracting amid surging prices.

tweets.text:
Ben Horowitz on the two skills that will matter more than ever before in an AI world: creativity and relationships.

"I think those are things that are hard to get out of today's AI in a very good way. So if you don't have instincts around those things, I don't know if all the AI in the world could help you. Whereas the grind-them-out tasks, AI is already really good at."

"Do you have original ideas? Can you establish and maintain very high quality, high fidelity relationships with people off the rip? I think people don't think about that enough."

"One big advantage I think that we have is we really look for that. Many just ignore that whole thing, like it's not a thing... It's a thing."

@bhorowitz w/ @Tocelot

A very strong El Nino is set to run into 2027.

Forecasters put overwhelming odds on a very strong El Nino persisting through winter, only fading toward neutral by the middle of 2027. That pattern reshapes global weather: drought in some breadbaskets, floods in others, and pressure on crops, energy demand, and shipping lanes.

Weather is a commodity input. A strong El Nino this long is a supply risk sitting under every food and energy price.

The 3.7% inflation scare is really an energy price shock.

Fuel oil is up 74% over the past year and gasoline 34%. Meanwhile eggs are down 21%, butter down 10%, smartphones down 10%, and used cars down 2%. Broad monetary inflation lifts everything at once. This move lifts energy and sinks half the shelf.

Price shocks fade. Money printing is what embeds inflation, and that is the number that actually matters. A Fed that hikes into an energy spike is fighting the wrong war.

Across 61 top business schools, more MBA programs saw their return on investment fall than rise from 2025 to 2026, on both the annualized return and the total 10-year dollar payoff. A few elite programs still added hundreds of thousands in lifetime value. Most moved the other way.

Across 61 top business schools, more MBA programs saw their return on investment fall than rise from 2025 to 2026, on both the annualized return and the total 10-year dollar payoff. A few elite programs still added hundreds of thousands in lifetime value. Most moved the other way.

When a name-brand MBA stops reliably paying for itself, the market is repricing what the credential is actually worth.

The melt-up just hit its first real air pocket.

The Nasdaq 100 fell more than 5% last week, its worst week since April 2025, as an AI selloff collided with oil near $110. Two shocks landed together: investors repricing the AI trade, and an energy price shock lifting costs across the economy.

The most expensive index has the least room to absorb either. When both hit at once, the air comes out of the top first.

$QQQ

tweets.text:
There is now $270 billion chasing a yield that keeps blowing up.

Derivative-income ETFs have exploded from barely $1 billion in 2020 to about $270 billion in 2026, more than doubling since 2024, as investors hunt for passive income. The problem is the product itself: you collect a rich distribution while the underlying price gets hammered.

Younger investors should own growth. Reaching for conservative income while risk-free Treasuries pay 5% is taking equity risk for no reason.

Refiners are printing money while drivers get squeezed.

The 321 crack spread, the margin for turning crude into gasoline and diesel, hit a record this quarter, topping the 2020 and 2022 peaks near $60 a barrel. When fuel-making margins blow out like this, the refiners capture the spread and every driver pays the other side.

An energy price shock always has a winner. Right now it is the refiner, not the pump.

$VLO

tweets.text:
High-beta surges in Tech stocks coincide with macro/EPS rebounds and broadenings, just like we've seen over the past 15 months. The other periods you can see here are: (working backwards) 20/21, 09, 03, 91,  and 87. Each beta unwind preceded a peak in eco/eps growth and breadth. As the cycle evolves, portfolio selection should too. Over the next year, we're unlikely to see the same increase in eco, earnings or expectations that we've enjoyed since mid-2025. Stock prices = outcome - expectations. In contrast to the past 15m or so, where broadly improving expectations drove a TREND in riskier stocks, the best bet for higher-beta stocks going forward is a short-term,  short-lived bounce following a sell off. My 2c. 
[chart of S&P 1500 Tech stocks l/s 1yr beta factor]
